Speaking on ["The Draymond Green Show"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MW4NApijsKU) as he discussed [Steph Curry's injury](https://www.nbcsportsbayarea.com/nba/golden-state-warriors/steph-curry-injury-houston-rockets/1979317/) and playing without him, Green addressed the label that followed the [Warriors' 115-108 loss](https://www.nbcsportsbayarea.com/nba/golden-state-warriors/steph-curry-injury-yaxel-lendeborg-houston-rockets/1979349/) in Houston on Nov. 11. Some fans blamed Sengun, yet Green explains the team is just outright physical, not dirty.
"I know a lot of people are saying, 'Oh man, the Houston Rockets are a dirty team.' I don't get off into that dirty thing," Green said. "Every now and then you see some people that just do things that are downright dirty, and it happens, and when it does, I'll speak on it."

Green drew a different line. He said the thing that bothers him most about Houston is not rough play.
"Do they do some bulls--- when we play them? Absolutely," Green said. "I think the thing that may irritate me the most is, like, they play super physical, but then they start flopping sometimes, you know. And so I would say that irritates me more, but I'm not going to sit here and call them a dirty team. They're a physical team."
Green said the film backs it up.
"When we were watching film pregame, you can see on the film they are physical as hell, and so give them credit," Green said.

Draymond Green said on the latest episode of his podcast, “The Draymond Green Show,” that he does not expect Stephen Curry back on the timeline the Golden State Warriors initially laid out for his oblique abdominal tear. “I would say there’s probably no chance that he’s back in two weeks,” Green said.
The Warriors announced Thursday, Nov. 12, that an MRI confirmed Curry’s oblique abdominal tear and that [he would be re-evaluated in two weeks](https://sideeyesports.com/2026/11/12/stephen-curry-is-expected-to-miss-closer-to-a-month-for-the-golden-state-warriors/). Green explained why that window is not a return date: “An oblique injury is one of those things that, like, tells you when it’s healed. There’s no certain timeline like it. Some of them heal faster than others depending on the severity, depending on where it could be.”
He added that core and rotational strength have to return gradually, and that “as the pain starts to subside, you start to push the boundaries more and more. But no one knows how long that’ll take.”

Green’s comments are not new medical information — he is not a doctor and was not relaying a team report. What they do is translate a vague “two-week re-evaluation” into a plainer warning that the real number is likely bigger, from someone who sees Curry every day.
## The Re-Evaluation Date Falls After Three More Games
The Warriors visit the New Orleans Pelicans on Monday, Nov. 16, before a back-to-back against the Dallas Mavericks and Memphis Grizzlies on Nov. 18 and 19. Curry’s own re-evaluation, per the Warriors’ timeline, falls around Nov. 26.

The Golden State [Warriors will have to play without Stephen Curry](https://clutchpoints.com/nba/golden-state-warriors/warriors-news-steve-kerr-reveal-next-date-stephen-curry-injury-update) for some time as he recovers from an oblique abdominal tear. This isn't the first time that the Warriors have had to do this, as Curry dealt with a knee issue that sidelined him for an extended period last season. The severity of that injury was recently explained by Curry, and he noted that he pushed through a lot of pain to play.
That comes as no surprise to some people, including [Draymond Green](https://clutchpoints.com/nba/players/a6200920/draymond-green), who probably knows him better than anyone at this point in his career. On his latest podcast episode, Green gave Curry props for [fighting through the injury](https://x.com/ClutchPoints/status/2123163619135238334).
“That's kind of expected, man. I know he had big issues, a lot of issues with the knee last year… And so I think for him, I think he loved the game of basketball… But needless to say, also one of the toughest players that you're going to come across, and if there's a way to play, he will be playing,” Green said.

ultimate.title: Draymond Green defends Rockets from ‘dirty' label after Steph Curry injury
ultimate.snippet:
Speaking on ["The Draymond Green Show"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MW4NApijsKU) as he discussed [Steph Curry's injury](https://www.nbcsportsbayarea.com/nba/golden-state-warriors/steph-curry-injury-houston-rockets/1979317/) and playing without him, Green addressed the label that followed the [Warriors' 115-108 loss](https://www.nbcsportsbayarea.com/nba/golden-state-warriors/steph-curry-injury-yaxel-lendeborg-houston-rockets/1979349/) in Houston on Nov. 11. Curry grimaced and reached for his right side after tangling with Rockets center [Alperen Sengun](https://www.basketball-reference.com/players/s/sengual01.html) on a screen early in the first quarter, leaving the game minutes later.
An MRI confirmed an oblique abdominal tear, and Curry will be re-evaluated in two weeks, with [ESPN's Shams Charania](https://x.com/ShamsCharania/status/2120971392678269219) reporting the team expects him to miss closer to a month. Some fans blamed Sengun, yet Green explains the team is just outright physical, not dirty.
"I know a lot of people are saying, 'Oh man, the Houston Rockets are a dirty team.' I don't get off into that dirty thing," Green said. "Every now and then you see some people that just do things that are downright dirty, and it happens, and when it does, I'll speak on it."

Green drew a different line. He said the thing that bothers him most about Houston is not rough play.
"Do they do some bulls--- when we play them? Absolutely," Green said. "I think the thing that may irritate me the most is, like, they play super physical, but then they start flopping sometimes, you know. And so I would say that irritates me more, but I'm not going to sit here and call them a dirty team. They're a physical team."
Green said the film backs it up.
"When we were watching film pregame, you can see on the film they are physical as hell, and so give them credit," Green said.

ultimate.snippet:
By

Days before the Warriors' road trip unraveled, Draymond Green explained on his show why Golden State is so dependent on Stephen Curry. When Curry is on the floor, he pulls two defenders away and gives the Warriors a four-on-three advantage, and without him, the team has to beat five defenders. 

The next five games proved the point, and Green did not hold back when he looked back on them.

"Arguably one of the worst stretches of basketball I've ever played in in my career," Green said on his podcast. He compared it to 2020, the season the Warriors fell to the bottom of the league, and said the effort was the part he found hardest to accept. "Our effort wasn't great. And that's disappointing, you know, our defense wasn't great, you know, and that's disappointing."

The record backs him up. Golden State entered the trip on an eight-game winning streak and finished it winless at 8-8. Curry left the opener against Houston with 6:25 left in the first quarter, and an MRI confirmed an oblique tear. The Warriors then lost to the Spurs 123-85, the Pelicans 115-94, the Mavericks 116-94 and the Grizzlies 126-98. They matched an unwanted franchise record from the 1997-98 season with four straight losses by at least 20 points.

Green was careful not to hide behind the injury. "Obviously, when Steph goes out, everything changes," he said, but he didn't treat that as an excuse. He believed the team could have controlled more, and he included himself in that. "There's a lot of things that we can control, that we can be better at, that we didn't control. And that's disappointing, that's on me."

His view is supported by the numbers beyond the scoreboard. The Warriors made 40 of 154 three-point attempts, or 26%, across the four full games without Curry. They also started slowly, averaging 18.5 first-quarter points while allowing 34.8. In San Antonio, they scored 14 first-quarter points while the Spurs opened with 18 unanswered.
